newsitem.title: USA: N. Dakota flood exodus continues in all directions.
newsitem.headline: N. Dakota flood exodus continues in all directions.

text.p: Weary residents continued to evacuate Grand Forks on Monday, travelling in all directions to flee a city ravaged by flood and fire.
Dozens of hamlets like Arvilla have opened their doors to complete strangers, offering up food, clothing and shelter to ease victims' burdens.

Linda Kram, her two daughters and her grandson met up Monday in Arvilla, about 20 miles west of Grand Forks. She has been staying at a nearby farm since she evacuated Saturday from her home of 25 years.
"We're thinking about going to California for a couple of weeks," Kram said. "We don't want to inconvenience the people we're staying with any more than we have to."
Kram reckoned her house will survive, and expected to find only knee-deep water in her basement.
"We feel pretty fortunate -- a lot more fortunate than a lot of others," Kram said.
Her daughter, Shelly Wurzbacher, feared her house had suffered a worse fate.
"From the pictures they're showing on TV, we think it's at least waist-high on the main floor," Wurzbacher said.

Officials estimated that between 90 and 95 percent of the city of 50,000 people had evacuated as of Monday, forced out after the swollen Red River burst through dikes and spilled into the pancake-flat streets.

Cindy Buckhouse, 34, fled her basement apartment Saturday along with her boyfriend, Mark Bjorgaard, and their cat. She said she had been searching for days for word from her parents, brother and sister, who all lost homes in the flood.
"You take it in stride. You can't do anything else," she said, shrugging when asked what she would do next.
Buckhouse moved to a more intimate shelter in Arvilla after finding the cavernous hangars at an Air Force Base crowded and intrusive.

Setting up the small shelter was partly the work of Marvis Paulson, a soils tester who spearheaded a drive to collect donations in this farm community. "These people need a lot more than food and shelter. They need jobs, recreation and to get in touch with their families," Paulson said.
Colin Hughes, 40, was one of the last holdouts in Grand Forks, choosing to evacuate his home Sunday only after it became clear he could beat the flood.

"I was the last man in my neighbourhood. I just couldn't stand it. I was too lonely," Hughes said as he, his wife and two daughters prepared to fly to Fort Lauderdale, Fla., for what was likely to be an extended stay.
